pos: proper n. (chamberlain of Herod Agrippa I)
etymology: Greek Blastos, a common Greek name meaning a sprout, a shoot.
biblical_def: Blastus was the man to know in Herod's court. Tyre and Sidon had offended the king, and they depended on his land for grain, so they came seeking peace, “having made Blastus the king's chamberlain their friend” (Acts 12:20). The diplomacy worked, and it led to the most public fall in the book of Acts. On a set day Herod made an oration, “And the people gave a shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man” (Acts 12:22). The flattery Blastus helped arrange was the flattery that killed his master: “And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost” (Acts 12:23). Luke sets the scene beside the church's answer, “But the word of God grew and multiplied” (Acts 12:24). The courtier's influence bought peace with a king; it could not buy the king a reprieve from God.

pos: proper n. (orator who accused Paul before Felix)
etymology: Latin Tertullus, a diminutive of Tertius, third; a Roman name borne by a professional advocate.
biblical_def: The Sanhedrin hired a lawyer. “And after five days Ananias the high priest descended with the elders, and with a certain orator named Tertullus, who informed the governor against Paul” (Acts 24:1). Tertullus opened with flattery of Felix, then turned to slander: “For we have found this man a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes” (Acts 24:5). It was a skilled speech and an empty one, and Paul answered it without a single compliment, laying out the facts and then confessing his faith openly: “But this I confess unto thee, that after the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers, believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets” (Acts 24:14). Tertullus had rhetoric; Paul had the truth and a good conscience. Felix deferred the case, and the gospel was preached before the governor.

pos: proper n. (centurion of Augustus’ band who brought Paul to Rome)
etymology: Latin Julius, the Roman family name of the Julian house, common among soldiers and freedmen.
biblical_def: Paul sailed for Rome as a prisoner in the charge of a soldier. “And when it was determined that we should sail into Italy, they delivered Paul and certain other prisoners unto one named Julius, a centurion of Augustus' band” (Acts 27:1). The centurion showed kindness from the first port: “And Julius courteously entreated Paul, and gave him liberty to go unto his friends to refresh himself” (Acts 27:3). At first he trusted the shipmaster over Paul, and the ship was lost; but when the soldiers proposed to kill the prisoners, the centurion stood between them and the sword: “But the centurion, willing to save Paul, kept them from their purpose; and commanded that they which could swim should cast themselves first into the sea, and get to land” (Acts 27:43). God had promised Paul that he would stand before Caesar, and He used a Roman officer's decency to keep the promise.

pos: proper n. (master of the eunuchs under Nebuchadnezzar)
etymology: Hebrew 'ashpenaz, probably from an Old Persian or Babylonian title or name; its meaning is uncertain.
biblical_def: Ashpenaz held the young exiles' lives in his hand. “And the king spake unto Ashpenaz the master of his eunuchs, that he should bring certain of the children of Israel, and of the king's seed, and of the princes” (Daniel 1:3). He gave them Babylonian names and set them on the king's meat. Then Daniel made his stand: “But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself” (Daniel 1:8). The request might have cost Daniel his life and Ashpenaz his head, but the text names the cause of the official's goodwill: “Now God had brought Daniel into favour and tender love with the prince of the eunuchs” (Daniel 1:9). Ashpenaz was a pagan officer, and God turned his heart as He turns the rivers of water.

pos: proper n. (officer set over Daniel and his companions)
etymology: Hebrew meltsar, with the article in the Hebrew text; probably an Akkadian title, guardian or steward, which the Authorized Version renders as a name.
biblical_def: Melzar was the man who actually served the four youths their meals. Daniel did not defy him; he proposed a test. “Then said Daniel to Melzar, whom the prince of the eunuchs had set over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah” (Daniel 1:11), and asked for ten days of pulse and water. At the end of the trial, “their countenances appeared fairer and fatter in flesh than all the children which did eat the portion of the king's meat” (Daniel 1:15). So the steward changed the diet for good: “Thus Melzar took away the portion of their meat, and the wine that they should drink; and gave them pulse” (Daniel 1:16). Daniel's way with Melzar is a model of conscientious obedience: respectful, reasonable, unbending on the point of principle, and leaving the result to God.

pos: proper n. (chamberlain of Ahasuerus who plotted against the king; also Bigthana)
etymology: Hebrew bigtan, also written bigtana', a Persian name, perhaps gift of God in the Persian sense. Bigthan of Esther 2:21 and Bigthana of Esther 6:2 are one man.
biblical_def: Bigthan's conspiracy is a hinge in the book of Esther. “In those days, while Mordecai sat in the king's gate, two of the king's chamberlains, Bigthan and Teresh, of those which kept the door, were wroth, and sought to lay hand on the king Ahasuerus” (Esther 2:21). Mordecai learned of it and told Esther, the plot was found out, “therefore they were both hanged on a tree: and it was written in the book of the chronicles before the king” (Esther 2:23). Nothing was done for Mordecai at the time. Years later, on the night before Haman meant to hang him, the king could not sleep, and the chronicles were read: “And it was found written, that Mordecai had told of Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's chamberlains” (Esther 6:2). God's name is not written in Esther, but His hand is on every page, and a traitor's failed plot became the hinge on which Mordecai was raised and Haman brought down.

Bigthan's plot is recorded so that it can be remembered at exactly the right hour.

pos: proper n. (steward of Herod Antipas, husband of Joanna)
etymology: Greek Chouzas, probably from an Aramaic or Nabataean name; its meaning is uncertain.
biblical_def: Chuza is named only as the husband of a disciple. Luke lists the women who followed Jesus through Galilee: “And certain women, which had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities, Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils” (Luke 8:2), “And Joanna the wife of Chuza Herod's steward, and Susanna, and many others, which ministered unto him of their substance” (Luke 8:3). The steward managed the household of the man who beheaded John the Baptist, and his wife spent her means on the Christ. Joanna was among the women at the empty tomb: “It was Mary Magdalene, and Joanna, and Mary the mother of James, and other women that were with them, which told these things unto the apostles” (Luke 24:10). The gospel reached into Herod's own house, and a high official's wife became one of the first witnesses of the resurrection.

pos: proper n. (paralytic at Lydda healed through Peter)
etymology: Greek Aineas, a Greek name made famous by Virgil's hero; probably related to aineo, to praise.
biblical_def: Peter came down to the saints at Lydda, “And there he found a certain man named Aeneas, which had kept his bed eight years, and was sick of the palsy” (Acts 9:33). The apostle did not pray at length or perform a ceremony. He named the Healer: “And Peter said unto him, Aeneas, Jesus Christ maketh thee whole: arise, and make thy bed. And he arose immediately” (Acts 9:34). Peter claimed no power of his own; the present tense puts the work in the hands of the risen Christ. The effect went beyond one man: “And all that dwelt at Lydda and Saron saw him, and turned to the Lord” (Acts 9:35). The miracle authenticated the apostolic word, and the word turned a whole district to Christ.

The apostolic signs were given to confirm the word of the apostles as they laid the foundation of the church (Hebrews 2:3-4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). The dictionary is cessationist: God still heals in answer to prayer, but the sign-gift of healing ceased with the apostolic age.
The principle to recover is the Name Peter used. Jesus Christ maketh thee whole: the apostle pointed away from himself to the risen Lord, and the purpose of the sign was that men should turn to Him.

pos: proper n. (Gideon’s servant on the night raid)
etymology: Hebrew purah, perhaps from pu'rah, a bough, a branch.
biblical_def: On the night before the battle, the LORD made a promise and then made allowance for Gideon's fear. “Arise, get thee down unto the host; for I have delivered it into thine hand” (Judges 7:9). “But if thou fear to go down, go thou with Phurah thy servant down to the host” (Judges 7:10). So master and servant crept to the edge of Midian's camp and heard a soldier tell his dream of a cake of barley bread tumbling into the camp. The effect on Gideon was immediate: “he worshipped, and returned into the host of Israel, and said, Arise; for the LORD hath delivered into your hand the host of Midian” (Judges 7:15). Phurah says nothing in the story. He is the companion God permitted to a trembling man, and his silent presence is part of God's patience with the weak faith of His servants.

pos: proper n. (the Bethelite who rebuilt Jericho)
etymology: Hebrew chi'el, probably a shortened form meaning God lives or brother of God.
biblical_def: Five centuries after Joshua laid a curse on Jericho, a man from Bethel tested it. Joshua had said: “Cursed be the man before the LORD, that riseth up and buildeth this city Jericho: he shall lay the foundation thereof in his firstborn, and in his youngest son shall he set up the gates of it” (Joshua 6:26). In the days of Ahab the word came due: “In his days did Hiel the Bethelite build Jericho: he laid the foundation thereof in Abiram his firstborn, and set up the gates thereof in his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by Joshua the son of Nun” (1 Kings 16:34). The verse stands at the close of the account of Ahab's accession, as a sign of what Israel had become: a people who treated God's word as an old story. Five hundred years had not weakened it. “God is not a man, that he should lie” (Numbers 23:19).
